figures.caption: A toy example showing how Sequent-Prover turns an underspecified commonsense claim into a grounded, checkable inconsistency.
figures.headline: A commonsense claim is turned into an SMT-LIB program whose Z3 run exposes a grounded inconsistency.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Post-training, especially DPO, shifts the models from merely sampling correct answers toward more reliable solver-grounded proof behavior. Hatched bars show each base checkpoint and colored overlays show the tuned-model gain: avg@N measures per-sample correctness, pass^k measures consistency by requiring all sampled trajectories to be correct, mean grounding measures how much of the problem is represented in SMT, and vcr_unsat measures correct answers backed by non-trivial UNSAT/refutation certificates. The remaining panels show the mechanism behind the gains: tuned models more often drive Z3 to UNSAT verdicts, avoid trivial SMT calls, and obtain more verified progress per tool call and per reasoning turn.
figures.headline: Tuned checkpoints raise per-sample correctness, consistency, grounding and UNSAT-backed correct answers over their base checkpoints.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Sequent-Prover overview. The agent formalizes a task in SMT-LIB, calls Z3 over several turns, and uses solver feedback until it finishes. Successful trajectories train SFT, and preferred versus rejected trajectories train DPO.
figures.headline: The agent calls Z3 over several turns, and successful trajectories feed supervised fine-tuning while preferred ones feed preference optimization.

abstract: We introduce Sequent-Prover, a family of verifier-using language-model agents, and the post-training framework that produces them. Agents reason in an executable SMT-LIB scratchpad: they write complete SMT-LIB programs, query Z3 across turns, inspect solver feedback, repair formalizations, and terminate with an explicit answer. Our recipe, verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation, bootstraps from a noisy teacher proposal policy by sampling multi-turn trajectories, retaining the successful tail that is correct, non-trivial, grounded, and executable, then applying supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level preference optimization. Because solver success alone does not guarantee semantic faithfulness, we evaluate task accuracy, k-sample reliability, and SMT program quality. Across 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per model family, post-training raises the 4B model’s per-attempt accuracy from 85.6% to 97.0% and four-sample all-correct reliability (pass^4) from 64.1% to 91.7%. It also reduces average SMT calls from 4.10 to 2.52 and tokens per attempt from 18.97k to 12.72k. Sequent-Prover agents give answers backed by executable formal artifacts.

sections.body:
The introduction argues that fluent reasoning is not executable evidence, and that solver access alone does not guarantee reliable reasoning because of the autoformalization gap. The authors sample candidate formalization traces, run them with Z3, reject malformed or vacuous artifacts, and convert the rest into supervised and preference training data.

The section lists four findings: post-training improves multi-sample consistency, supervised fine-tuning yields better grounded SMT-LIB programs, post-training strengthens refutational unsat reasoning, and preference optimization adds gains in stability, grounding, and efficiency beyond supervised fine-tuning. These are stated as claims here; the detailed numbers appear in the results section.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Solver access alone does not ensure reliable reasoning, so the paper trains models to build grounded SMT-LIB formalizations across multi-turn Z3 use.

sections.body:
Verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation has three stages. First, a teacher model samples multi-turn rollouts through the same `z3-solve` and `finish` interface used at evaluation. Second, an acceptance predicate keeps rollouts that reach the correct answer and show executable, non-trivial, input-grounded solver evidence; these are labeled Gold. Correct but weakly supported rollouts are Silver, and failing rollouts are Rejected.

Third, the student is trained by supervised fine-tuning on Gold traces and by preference optimization on pairs that contrast Gold traces with Silver or Rejected ones. The teacher sees only the problem, not the target answer, so it is a stochastic proposal distribution rather than an oracle annotator.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Verifier-conditioned trajectory distillation keeps only correct, grounded, executable solver traces and trains on them with supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization.

sections.body:
The evaluation covers nine checkpoints (base, supervised, and preference-optimized) across three model families, with K=4 trajectories per problem over 37 benchmarks and 7,254 problems per family. For the 4B family, average per-attempt accuracy (avg@N) rises from 0.856 to 0.970 and pass^4 from 0.641 to 0.917, a 27.7-point gain in all-sample reliability. For 9B, pass^4 rises from 0.858 to 0.934, and the 27B base reaches pass^4 of 0.986 after tuning.

Table 2(a) shows that for the 4B preference-optimized model, 86.7% of 2,379 partially correct base problems become correct on all four tuned attempts. A single 4B preference-optimized sample matches the 4B base model's four-sample coverage. The 27B base has only 153 partially correct problems, so its gains are smaller.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Post-training raises the 4B model's average per-attempt accuracy from 0.856 to 0.970 and pass^4 from 0.641 to 0.917.

sections.body:
This section places the work among four lines of prior research: verifier-integrated theorem proving (Goedel Prover, DeepSeek-Prover, Kimina-Prover), solver-based symbolic reasoning with Z3 and cvc5, self-repair from execution or tool feedback, and reinforcement learning for verifiable outputs. The authors state that they shift the target language from Lean to SMT-LIB and focus on compact models that must operate across multiple SMT logics.

The section distinguishes its setting from classical symbolic systems: the language model is the primary generator, while the solver validates outputs and synthesizes extra training data. It says solver feedback is more structured than free-form critique, and that because repair is serial, improving expected solver reward is particularly useful. No experiments are reported here.
sections.heading: Related Works
sections.headline: Prior work in theorem proving, solver synthesis, tool feedback and reinforcement learning motivates the SMT-LIB target and solver-native repair.

sections.body:
The conclusion states that solver use can be learned as a formal-reasoning policy. Trajectories are filtered by executable SMT feedback, and successful traces are contrasted against failed ones, so the model learns to formulate proof obligations, encode them in SMT-LIB, interpret Z3 responses, repair artifacts, and commit with evidence.

The authors claim that post-training turns sample-dependent solver successes into stable behavior, produces more grounded and non-vacuous SMT programs, and shifts correct traces toward refutational unsat evidence. They say the gains are largest when a base model has latent solver-use competence but lacks consistency. The section reports no new measurements.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Solver use can be learned as a formal-reasoning policy that turns sample-dependent successes into stable, grounded and refutational behavior.

sections.body:
The limitations section states that a solver can check a formal artifact but cannot decide whether the chosen abstraction is the intended one. Most tasks have no reference formalization. The section notes that semantic equivalence is co-NP-complete in propositional logic and undecidable in first-order logic, so no automatic check can certify meaning preservation.

The authors use grounding, non-triviality, and structural-uncertainty measures, described in Appendix D.4, as strong proxies rather than proof of faithfulness. The section states that learning the right level of formal abstraction remains an open problem.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: A solver can check a formal artifact but cannot confirm the abstraction is the intended one, so semantic faithfulness stays unverified.

sections.body:
The appendix gives background on Z3's sat and unsat modes and on the tool-calling agent loop, which stops after `T_max`=10 turns. Each solver call runs under a 30-second wall-clock cap and a 256-MB memory cap. The training set has 14,307 samples: 10,785 Gold, 2,995 Rejected, 464 Silver, and 63 discarded infrastructure-error trajectories, generated by a Deepseek-v4 Flash teacher at temperature 0.9.

Table 8 reports the teacher's pass^3 as 0.484 on AR-LSAT, 0.738 on FOLIO, and 0.901 on ZebraLogic. Worked examples compare base and tuned agents on a self-contradiction diagnosis and on repairing solver error text.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists Z3 proof modes, the agent loop, datasets, training details, teacher accuracy, and worked solver trajectories.
